title: Cuba details: Mayor Morrison, other bands, modern touches
summary: Five days in Cuba, the parade plus three sessions including one for the mayor. Roy Liberto's group rode a float; Zanco says today's bands add a modern touch, except Chris Barber.

story.theme_name: Going abroad: American jazz musicians touring and living in Europe
story.community_name: Going abroad: touring Europe and Japan

blocks.x: Well, back to the straws, how many days were you in Cuba you say?
We were down there five days. Five days? Yeah.
And how many jobs did you play?

Well, we went down there primarily for this parade, you see, this carnival parade. But while we were down there, the mayor, Mayor Morrison, had some sort of a party over there, you know, for his personal friends and he invited the band to play, see, so he used our band. All in all, I would say we made about three sessions other than the parade, see. We had a session going up in our hotel room one night and I think that was the best music we'd ever played. Of course nobody was there to listen to us but it really came through great, you know.
Were there any other bands from new audience down there?
Yeah, they had, Hector Fontana had a group over there and, oh this one boy was playing over at the dream room, not the dream room, a famous duo. Trumpet player?

Roy Liberto, yeah, Roy Liberto. His group was over there. Incidentally, the other, Roy Liberto's group rode a float in the parade. They had some of the floats from the New Orleans Mardi Gras that was sent over there to go in this parade and Roy Liberto's group rode one of the floats. I don't know if Hector Fontana's band participated in the parade but they did some, you know, some of the extra parties and things like that. Our group, of course, had a march but all in all it was a real colorful parade. I think they had just about every country represented each, you know, country brought their own contingent or what would you call it. And it was a very colorful parade.
Did any of the other bands sound like jazz at all?

Uh, yeah, but I don't know, it seems to me that most, most of the, I don't know if I should be saying this, but most of the groups you hear now always seem to sneak in a modern touch somewhere along the line. You know, I mean, you just don't really hear that old, old brand of music. You hear jazz bands, you hear jazz tunes, but I don't know, maybe it's my ear, I don't know. But they just don't seem to have that crude sound as the old band had years ago, you know.
Well, I think the Englishmen have some of that.

Uh, speaking of Englishmen, there's this guy Chris Barber, I caught his show, you know, when he was at the auditorium. Boy, they, they were really hot stuff. They, now they produced pretty much of that real old sound.
Mm-hmm. How about any of the bands, not from your audience that were in Cuba, did they play any kind of, with a jazz feeling?

Well, uh, they were mostly, uh, school bands. Uh, I think, uh, one, one contingent over there was supposed to be a police band from some police department, I don't know where. But, uh, they played, uh, mostly parade and march stuff, you know. But, naturally, uh, representing New Orleans, we had to play jazz. We hardly knew any other music, see, we had to play jazz. Well, I, I should speak for myself then when I say hardly know any other music. I don't know hardly any other music. I just want to get the facts.
